summary: High Point's 1912 wood lookout gave way to a steel Aermotor tower in 1919; it closed in 1971, was removed in 1988, and footings remained in 2017.

facts.design: Steel Aermotor LS40 tower erected in 1919, replacing a 1912 wood tower
facts.status_note: Tower removed in 1988; footings and some telephone poles were still there on a 2017 visit.

events.note: The Conservation Commission established a lookout station at High Point and built a wood tower; the FFLA newsletter says the first tower was made of trees.
The commission announced an appointment for District No. 5, High Point Mountain: William Bradford of Ellenville.
A steel Aermotor LS40 tower was erected on the site, replacing the 1912 wood tower.
A new observer's cabin was erected at High Point, per the commission's annual report as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page.
The tower was decommissioned; it ceased fire lookout operation at the end of the 1971 season.
The steel tower was removed in 1988.
Spring 2015 fire on the ridge burned over 2,000 acres; the newsletter counts three major fires along the Ridge in ten years.
An FFLA group visiting in fall 2017 found the footings and some old telephone poles at the site.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The FFLA newsletter says the tower was decommissioned in 1971; Wikipedia says its last operations were at the end of the 1971 season. The two agree.
The newsletter says the 1912 tower was made of trees; Wikipedia says it was a wood fire lookout tower. The story says wood.

notes_for_editor: The brief has no height. Wikipedia's Shawangunk Ridge article gives the 1919 tower as 47 ft; no other source read gives a height, so the story gives none. The brief's 'only footings and old phone poles remain' is stronger than the newsletter, which reports footings and some poles seen on a fall 2017 visit; no later site report was found. The park named only as 'the Park' in the 2018 newsletter is not identified in the text read. Mapcarta is a crowd-sourced map listing and is used only for the 'ruins' classification. An FFLA NYS Facebook post about this site appeared in search (a snippet places the tower about 1,500 ft north of the summit on a spur) but the page did not yield readable text, so it is not used. Public access status was not established, so no access fact is recorded.
